subject: Career
title: The Mere Exposure Effect in Hiring
description: Learn The Mere Exposure Effect in Hiring in one minute.

hook.text: Candidates who've interacted with the company before get hired more often. Familiarity breeds preference.

buildup.text: The mere exposure effect: we prefer things we've seen before, even without conscious memory.

discovery.text: Commenting on company posts, attending events, or emailing the team creates prior exposure.

twist.text: This isn't manipulation — it's how human brains work. Familiarity feels like trust.

climax.text: By the time you walk in, you're not a stranger. You're someone they've already chosen to notice.

punchline.text: Be familiar before you're a candidate.

quiz.question: What is the mere exposure effect?
options: We prefer things we've encountered before

details.summary: The mere exposure effect means people develop preferences for things they encounter repeatedly. In hiring, candidates who have had prior touchpoints such as networking events, referrals, or informational interviews receive warmer evaluations.
details.whyItMatters: Creating familiarity before the formal interview gives you a psychological head start. It shifts the dynamic from evaluating a stranger to reconnecting with someone known.
takeaways: Three to five touchpoints before an interview significantly boost familiarity
LinkedIn engagement and event attendance create passive exposure
Referrals leverage the exposure effect through association

faq.question: How many touchpoints with a company are optimal before a formal interview?
faq.answer: Three to five is the sweet spot. This might include attending a company event, connecting with employees on LinkedIn, having an informational interview, and submitting a thoughtful application. More than five risks seeming overeager.

faq.question: Does the mere exposure effect work with virtual interactions as well?
faq.answer: Yes. Commenting thoughtfully on company posts, attending virtual events, and exchanging emails all create exposure. The effect is about repeated positive encounters, not physical proximity. Digital touchpoints are equally effective.
